title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 33–34
description: Advanced environmental threats, sustainable-development vocabulary and word families, plus nuanced descriptions of customer service, complaints and online retail.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Vocabulary targets were checked against teaching pages, exercise pages and the answer key; all English examples and explanatory notes and all Portuguese translations were independently authored. Original exercises, illustrations and extended textbook passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 33 environmental collocations, labelled footnotes, newspaper-style response phrases, Common mistakes and exercises 33.1–33.4; Unit 34 good and bad service, online customer-service expressions, exercises 34.1–34.3 and their answer keys.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA supplied selectively for short targets where the transcription was reasonably certain. Blank IPA is deliberate when stress or pronunciation has not been independently verified; no audio recordings were included.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing language is English except for the Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Read and visually checked PDF study and exercise pages, compared relevant answer-key entries, edited examples and notes independently and performed programmatic checks of schema parity, IDs, metadata, field types, TTS targets, and provenance. No live VocabLab import, browser TTS or speech-recognition test was run.
audit.limitations: No MP3 files accompany this package. Import compatibility is checked statically only; actual VocabLab import, browser TTS rendering and pronunciation recognition remain untested. Terminology may have additional specialist nuances beyond the source.

units.title: Unit 33 — Our endangered world
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 72–73 (PDF pages 74–75).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Environment · advanced environmental collocations and policy language
learningObjectives: Use precise collocations for threats to biodiversity, resource scarcity, pollution and climate change.
Describe environmental risk and uncertainty using demographic projections, worst-case scenarios and related terminology.
Discuss policy responses using sustainable development, renewable energy and green credentials.
Build relevant word families and avoid the uncountable-noun mistake in cause damage to the environment.

sectionsChecked: A · Threats and potential threats, numbered explanations and collocations
B · Responses to environmental issues, headlines and Common mistakes

items.pt: habitats cada vez menores; habitats em redução
items.example: Road building has left several endangered mammals with shrinking habitats.
items.note: Shrinking conveys a continuing reduction in the space available to a species.

items.example: The protected wetlands support remarkable biodiversity.
items.note: Refers to the variety of life, not simply the total number of individual animals.

items.example: Strict regulations aim to protect endangered species from illegal hunting.
items.note: Endangered indicates a risk of extinction; species is the same in the singular and plural.

items.pt: cético quanto às mudanças climáticas; pessoa que questiona as mudanças climáticas
items.example: The report addresses arguments raised by climate change sceptics.
items.note: British spelling: sceptic. This describes a position; it does not indicate that scientific evidence is evenly divided.

items.example: Long-term global warming poses serious risks to coastal communities.
items.note: The long-term increase in average global temperatures, not an unusually hot day.

items.example: Researchers monitored changes in polar ice using satellite measurements.
items.note: Refers to ice in polar regions; sea ice and land ice have different effects on sea levels.

items.example: Low-lying islands face increasing risks from rising sea levels.
items.note: A common environmental collocation; sea level is often singular in the phrase sea-level rise.

items.example: The transport authority published its annual carbon dioxide emissions data.
items.note: Emissions are gases released into the atmosphere; carbon dioxide is often abbreviated CO2 in writing.

items.example: The city is investing in alternatives to fossil fuels.
items.note: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels; they are not renewable on human timescales.

items.example: Extra greenhouse gases intensify the greenhouse effect.
items.note: The natural heat-trapping process is essential to life, but its intensification contributes to warming.

items.example: Rapid population growth has increased demand for housing and water.
items.note: Refers to an increase in population size, rather than necessarily an increase in density.

items.pt: exercer forte pressão sobre; sobrecarregar seriamente
items.example: Prolonged drought can exert severe pressure on regional water supplies.
items.note: Formal collocation: exert pressure on a system, resource or decision-maker.

items.example: The policy recognises that minerals are finite resources.
items.note: Finite resources exist in limited quantities and may be exhausted.

items.example: Removing a predator may disturb the ecological balance of an island.
items.note: Describes interactions that allow an ecosystem to function, not a perfectly static state.

items.example: Uncontrolled deforestation has damaged watersheds in the region.
items.note: Deforestation means clearing forests; uncontrolled stresses the lack of effective limits.

items.example: Long-term demographic projections inform decisions about public services.
items.note: Forecasts concerning populations and their characteristics, based on assumptions rather than certainties.

items.example: The number of simulated cases grew exponentially during the initial phase.
items.note: In technical usage, the growth rate is proportional to the existing amount; do not use for every rapid increase.

items.example: The report warns that the region is relying on depleting resources.
items.note: Depleting means becoming progressively less available.

items.pt: descarte de resíduos; destinação de lixo
items.example: Improper waste disposal has contaminated the nearby river.
items.note: Disposal is the process of getting rid of waste; it is not the same as reducing its production.

items.example: Toxic waste must be handled under strict safety procedures.
items.note: Toxic means poisonous or capable of causing serious harm.

items.example: Chemical runoff can contaminate groundwater.
items.note: Often used of pollution that makes water, soil or food unsafe.

items.pt: recurso precioso; bem de grande valor
items.example: Clean drinking water is becoming a precious commodity in arid regions.
items.note: Commodity is usually a resource or tradeable product; precious stresses its great value.

items.pt: segurança hídrica; garantia de acesso à água
items.example: New reservoirs are part of the region's long-term water security plan.
items.note: Water security concerns reliable access to sufficient safe water, not just water quality.

items.example: In the worst-case scenario, the entire harvest could fail.
items.note: A fixed compound used for the least favourable plausible outcome; hyphenate worst-case before scenario.

items.example: The organisation campaigns to preserve pristine environments from development.
items.note: Pristine suggests largely undamaged or unspoilt natural conditions.

items.example: The company wants to improve its green credentials by cutting emissions.
items.note: Usually means perceived environmental responsibility; claims need not prove actual performance.

items.pt: profetas do desastre; pessoas excessivamente pessimistas
items.example: Critics dismissed the analysts as prophets of doom and gloom.
items.note: A dismissive expression for people who predict bleak outcomes; can carry a negative judgement.

items.example: The municipal plan links economic growth with sustainable development.
items.note: Development intended to remain viable without undermining future environmental and social well-being.

items.example: The utility expanded its investment in renewable energy.
items.note: Energy derived from naturally replenished sources, such as sunlight and wind.

items.example: Poorly planned construction can cause damage to the environment.
items.note: Damage is uncountable in this use: avoid damages when referring generally to environmental harm.

items.example: The valley has distinctive climatic conditions.
items.note: Adjective related to climate; distinguish climatic from climactic, which relates to a climax.

items.example: The research combines geography with demography to predict regional needs.
items.note: The study of populations and their statistical characteristics.

items.example: The survey revealed significant demographic differences between districts.
items.note: Adjective meaning relating to population data or population groups.

items.example: The two cities are demographically quite different.
items.note: Adverb describing an assessment in terms of population characteristics.

items.example: The population projection assumes a gradual decline in birth rates.
items.note: In this unit, a forecast inferred from current trends and stated assumptions.

items.pt: projetar; prever com base em dados
items.example: The agency projects a moderate increase in urban demand.
items.note: Verb meaning forecast; stress is on the second syllable, unlike the noun project.

items.pt: sustentar; manter ao longo do tempo
items.example: The wetlands cannot sustain such intensive water extraction.
items.note: Means support or maintain something over time; may describe ecosystems or economic activity.

items.example: The committee assessed the sustainability of the proposed development.
items.note: Noun for the capacity to continue without exhausting necessary resources or causing unacceptable harm.

items.example: The university introduced a more sustainable procurement policy.
items.note: Able to continue over time without undermining the resources or conditions that support it.

items.example: Laboratory tests identified contamination in several soil samples.
items.note: Noun derived from contaminate; commonly used of water, soil, food and air.

items.example: Residents were advised not to drink the contaminated water.
items.note: Describes material made unsafe or impure by a contaminant.

items.example: The researchers measured toxin levels in the shellfish.
items.note: A poisonous substance, often one produced by a living organism.

items.example: The laboratory recorded a toxic concentration of the chemical.
items.note: Adjective related to harmful poisonous substances.

items.example: Groundwater depletion threatens farming in the valley.
items.note: The process of reducing a resource, often through prolonged use.

items.example: Excessive pumping could deplete the aquifer.
items.note: Transitive verb: deplete reserves, stocks or resources.

items.example: The report warns that uncontrolled dumping could lead to an environmental catastrophe.
items.note: A very serious event or outcome causing extensive environmental damage.

items.example: The spill caused irreparable damage to a fragile coastal habitat.
items.note: Damage is uncountable here; irreparable means it cannot be put right.

items.example: The writer links overpopulation to pressure on the city's housing stock.
items.note: A situation where population is considered too large for available resources or infrastructure.

units.title: Unit 34 — Here to help: customer service
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 74–75 (PDF pages 76–77).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Customer service · quality, complaints and digital transactions
learningObjectives: Contrast positive customer-service qualities such as responsive, accommodating and obliging with negative descriptions.
Use precise collocations for delays, telephone support, warranties and order fulfilment.
Discuss online accounts, security, browsing, order tracking and in-store service.
Recognise additional online shop interface vocabulary from the exercises, including returns policies, site maps and baskets.

sectionsChecked: A · Good service and annotated expressions
B · Bad service, service delays and guarantees
C · Service encounters on the internet

items.pt: uma resposta rápida; uma resposta sem demora
items.example: Customers should receive a prompt reply to every written complaint.
items.note: Prompt means without unnecessary delay; reply to a query or complaint.

items.example: Our support team answered the technical query within an hour.
items.note: A request for information, common in professional and customer-service contexts.

items.pt: atento às reclamações; que reage prontamente às reclamações
items.example: The provider was responsive to complaints about the faulty equipment.
items.note: Be responsive to something: listen and react constructively; to is essential.

items.example: The hotel staff were accommodating when we requested a quieter room.
items.note: Willing to adapt to reasonable needs; not about providing accommodation here.

items.pt: retornar o contato com alguém; dar uma resposta a alguém
items.example: I will get back to you once the replacement is confirmed.
items.note: Means reply or make contact later; different from physically returning somewhere.

items.example: The independent shop is known for its impeccable service.
items.note: Impeccable is a strong positive evaluation: faultless or exceptionally good.

items.example: The receptionist was obliging and found us an earlier appointment.
items.note: A positive adjective for someone willing to assist; often used of staff.

items.example: The technician was incompetent and made the fault worse.
items.note: Describes insufficient ability or skill, rather than simply unfriendly behaviour.

items.example: Automated replies made the whole experience feel impersonal.
items.note: Indicates lack of a personal, human approach; not necessarily technically incorrect.

items.example: The contractor apologised for the shoddy repair work.
items.note: Disapproving word for poor-quality goods or workmanship; stronger than merely ordinary.

items.pt: abaixo do padrão esperado; de qualidade inferior
items.example: The regulator criticised the company's substandard maintenance procedures.
items.note: Below an expected or required level of quality; common in formal criticism.

items.pt: pouco colaborativo; que se recusa a cooperar
items.example: The agent was uncooperative when we asked for a written explanation.
items.note: Unwilling to assist or work with someone; contrasts with accommodating and obliging.

items.example: The warehouse is working through a backlog of orders after the holiday.
items.note: Backlog means work waiting to be dealt with, not orders already completed.

items.pt: senso de urgência; percepção de prioridade
items.example: The support team showed little sense of urgency despite the outage.
items.note: Having a sense of urgency means recognising the need to act promptly.

items.example: Being transferred between departments was exasperating.
items.note: Causes intense frustration or irritation; distinguish from exasperated, which describes the person feeling it.

items.pt: linha telefônica de apoio; canal de atendimento por telefone
items.example: The bank operates a helpline for customers whose cards have been lost.
items.note: Traditionally a telephone service for assistance; other channels may now coexist.

items.pt: colocar alguém em espera durante uma ligação
items.example: The operator put me on hold while checking the order number.
items.note: Phone expression; differs from putting a project on hold, meaning suspending it.

items.example: The replacement part was still under guarantee when it failed.
items.note: British customer-service phrase meaning that a repair or replacement promise still applies.

items.example: The device was repaired free of charge because it was under warranty.
items.note: Warranty and guarantee overlap, but precise legal coverage varies by product and jurisdiction.

items.pt: site seguro; site com conexão protegida
items.example: Only enter payment details through a secure site.
items.note: Here secure refers to safeguards for transmitted information; it is not a guarantee that a merchant is trustworthy.

items.pt: criar uma conta; cadastrar uma conta
items.example: You need to set up an account before placing your first order.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: set an account up or set it up.

items.example: Read the privacy policy before agreeing to share personal data.
items.note: A document describing how an organisation handles personal information.

items.example: The retailer uses encryption to support secure transactions.
items.note: The source uses secure for protected business exchanges, especially payment information.

items.example: You can check availability for the dates you want before booking.
items.note: Common phrase for confirming whether a room, product or service can be supplied.

items.example: The updated delivery schedule is linked from the home page.
items.note: The introductory or main page of a website; distinct from its other individual pages.

items.pt: perguntas frequentes; seção de dúvidas frequentes
items.example: The FAQ explains how to request a refund.
items.note: Stands for frequently asked questions; the book specifies letter-by-letter pronunciation.

items.example: You can browse the catalogue without creating an account.
items.note: Browse means look through options; it does not imply making a purchase.

items.example: The site index helped us locate the warranty information.
items.note: An organised list of website content; this term is less prominent on many modern websites.

items.example: The seller promised immediate dispatch once the payment cleared.
items.note: Dispatch means sending goods out; it does not guarantee immediate delivery.

items.example: The supplier offers a nationwide service through regional partners.
items.note: Nationwide means covering a whole country, unlike local or regional service.

items.example: Customers can track their order from dispatch to delivery.
items.note: Track means monitor progress or location; a common online retail interface phrase.

items.pt: na loja física; presencialmente na loja
items.example: Certain discounts are available in-store but not online.
items.note: Contrasts shopping in a physical retail location with online shopping.

items.example: The returns policy explains which items can be sent back for a refund.
items.note: An online shop's rules and conditions for returning purchased goods.

items.example: The site map lists all the main sections of the portal.
items.note: An overview of website sections and their organisation, which may be visual or textual.

items.example: Add the item to your shopping basket before proceeding to checkout.
items.note: The exercise uses basket for goods selected online but not yet bought; cart is also common.

items.pt: cookies; pequenos arquivos de rastreamento ou preferências
items.example: The website asks visitors to choose which cookies they allow.
items.note: Small pieces of data stored by a website or browser; not all cookies are for tracking.

items.example: Customers can browse categories to compare similar products.
items.note: Combines the source verb browse with the exercise's navigation label.

items.pt: de relance; com uma rápida olhada
items.example: The dashboard shows delivery status at a glance.
items.note: A set phrase meaning very quickly and without detailed examination.
